home.heroBody:
I'm a financial adviser who came from a background in design and product. Today I share knowledge about Singapore insurance, savings, retirement and family protection on Xiaohongshu and WeChat Channels.

I'm not one to push for a sale. I'd rather make the complex products, fine print and cash flows genuinely clear — so that the people who truly need cover can choose with full understanding.

Every family's income, responsibilities, risk appetite and goals are different. My job isn't to get you to buy more, but to help you see clearly: what must come first, what can wait, and what you simply don't need.

about.title: Yuan Yuan
about.subtitle: Yuan Yuan SG · Building wealth with you, steadily
about.intro: I'm Yuan Yuan, an AIA Wealth Manager in Singapore and an MDRT member. Licensed in 2024, in under two years I've planned insurance and finances for families from Singapore, Malaysia, Australia, Turkey and beyond. Their backgrounds differ, but their hope is the same: to put down roots here and live with peace of mind. I believe wealth isn't built overnight, but through the right plan — year after year.
about.section1Title: From product design to wealth management
about.section1Body:
I didn't start out in this field.

After graduating from Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications in 2013, I came to Singapore for a Master's in Digital Media Technology at NTU. For nearly a decade after, I worked as a product designer —

At DeNA, a leading Japanese mobile game company, I ran planning and operations for a Marvel game, coordinating across Tokyo, Singapore, Hanoi and North America. At Great Eastern, Singapore's largest insurer, I led a six-person UX team in redesigning the official app and online claims system for 2.5 million policyholders. Later I joined the Southeast Asian super-app Grab, leading design for the GrabFood merchant platform and GrabExpress.

Through all of it, I kept one habit: no matter how busy, I always made time to document and reflect. It's what let me see my own path clearly at every turning point.
about.section2Body:
If you've seen my résumé, this might surprise you: why would someone with nearly a decade in product design — at DeNA, Great Eastern, Grab — turn to insurance?

It starts with a prejudice.

Before entering this field, I knew nothing about insurance and was, frankly, biased against it — I thought of it as a sales pitch, a favour, a tangle of fine print. Then, during my years at Great Eastern, I designed the company's customer app and online claims system, walked through the entire journey from application to claim, and personally interviewed hundreds of policyholders, agents and claims staff.

I saw the industry as it really is: many people buy insurance yet never understand what they're actually covered for; many practitioners favour marketing over service, acquisition over after-care — once a policy is sold, the client can't find them again. Behind that mess lies countless families' misunderstanding of, and disappointment with, the word "protection."

In 2023, returning from maternity leave at Grab, my department was dissolved. Rather than rush to the next job, I used the pause to seriously consider what I wanted. A seasoned career coach, after getting to know me, suggested something unexpected: become a wealth adviser. She said I was gentle, methodical, numbers-sensitive and logical — exactly the foundation this work needs.

In that moment I felt a strange sense of destiny: wasn't I once exactly the person who was biased against insurance? If even I could be won over by genuinely professional, genuinely client-first service, couldn't I become that kind of adviser too — and change how more people see this industry?

So I chose AIA, and a team whose client-first philosophy matched my own. My approach is simple: no cold pitching, no pestering friends. When I'm not with clients, I spend my time sharing real, useful knowledge on social media, and let the people who need me come to me. Earning clients this way means I have to be genuinely good — that's the only way to be seen and trusted.

And it works — in my first year, on word of mouth and referrals alone, I earned MDRT membership.
about.section3Title: Building a reputation through professionalism and care
about.section3Body:
My approach is simple: move forward in small, solid steps.

I'm not chasing speed. I'm chasing the day when, years from now, a client mentioned in passing can say with conviction: "Oh, Yuan Yuan — she's a trustworthy, dependable adviser who really knows her stuff."
about.mediaBody: I don't like to intrude — but I'm far from passive. When I'm not with clients, I do one thing: take the complex, easily-misunderstood parts of insurance and finance, and explain them in plain language anyone can follow.

cases.title: Real planning, real considerations
cases.intro: The following are anonymised summaries of real client situations. All identifying details have been removed and figures masked; they're shared only to illustrate the planning approach.
cases.msNote: Every plan I make follows the basic financial-planning principles of MoneySense, by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) — protection first, then growth, always within your means.
cases.disclaimer: What suits one person may not suit you. Every family is different, and specific arrangements can only be determined after a full needs analysis.

list.tag: New to the workforce · Laying the foundation
list.title: A single 25-year-old, newly arrived in Singapore
list.profile: 25, single, EP holder, newly joined a local tech firm, annual income around S$9***. On her own in Singapore, parents back home, no dependants.
list.existing: Company group medical (basic, lapses on leaving), no personal policies.
list.risk: Conservative. Few savings so far; her main concern is "not letting one illness or accident derail everything."
list.needs: Cover the most basic health and accident risks on a limited budget, without tying up too much cash flow.
list.advice: MoneySense is clear for this stage (19–29): build an emergency fund first, then spend no more than 15% of income on protection. I mapped out three foundational layers: (1) an Integrated Shield Plan — the bedrock, portable and lifelong, around 2*** a year; (2) personal accident cover — excellent value for an active young adult, just 2*** a year; (3) early critical-illness cover — locking in around S$10**** while young and rates are low, around 2*** a year. I recommended no savings or investment products at this stage — for her, the smartest "investment" is locking in health cover at a low rate while young.

list.tag: Rising responsibility · Protecting the home and each other
list.title: Newlyweds who just bought a home (30)
list.profile: Both 30 — one PR, one citizen, dual income, household income around S$18****. Newly married, just bought a home with a mortgage of about S$60****.
list.existing: Each has hospitalisation and accident cover (arranged before marriage); no critical illness, no life cover.
list.risk: Conservative. Their biggest worry: "if one of us goes down, can we keep the house?"
list.needs: Ensure that if one passes away or falls seriously ill, the mortgage won't crush the other; close the critical-illness gap.
list.advice: The foundation was in place; the gap was in "family responsibility." By MAS rules of thumb — death/TPD cover around 9× annual income, critical illness around 4× — I added two pieces: (1) mortgage-reducing term assurance — purpose-built to offset mortgage risk, covering the outstanding balance and reducing alongside it, one each, around 2*** a year; should the worst happen, the payout clears the mortgage directly; (2) critical-illness cover — around S$20**** each, so that if one falls ill, there's money to replace income and cover recovery. Total premiums kept within 15% of household income.

list.tag: A new life · A first layer of protection and a future
list.title: A family welcoming a newborn (33)
list.profile: Parents around 33, settled in Singapore, household income around S$20****. Baby just born; the parents' own cover is fairly complete, and focus has shifted to the child.
list.existing: Both parents have hospitalisation, accident and critical-illness cover; the child has none yet.
list.risk: Conservative, willing to plan long-term for the child.
list.needs: Basic health cover for the newborn; a long-term, steady plan for the child's future education fund.
list.advice: For newborns, earlier is better — simpler underwriting and lower rates. Two steps: First (priority), the baby's basic health cover — child hospitalisation around 2***, child accident around 2***, and optionally child critical illness locking in around S$10**** at a lifelong low rate. Second (the core goal), a long-term education savings plan — for the funding needs around age 18, contributing around 2*** a year to provide a relatively certain cash flow when it's needed (non-guaranteed portions per the policy illustration). One thing I stressed: the child's cover matters, but make sure the parents' own cover is sufficient first — parents are the child's biggest "policy." That's the order MoneySense consistently emphasises.

list.tag: Stability first · Turning idle funds into a flexible arrangement
list.title: A risk-averse 40-year-old executive · USD savings plan
list.profile: 40, senior executive at a major firm, stable career, peak earning years. Married, one or two children, ageing parents. Around US$50**** available to plan — funds not needed in the short term.
list.existing: Company group medical, basic hospitalisation, some life/critical-illness cover, basic accident cover.
list.risk: Low. Not chasing short-term swings; values certainty and the ability to access funds when needed.
list.needs: A long-term, stable future cash flow; stability with future flexibility; if his career pace changes, an arrangement he can start early; and the ability to pass wealth to family.
list.advice: His protection layer was complete; the need was clear — not to chase returns, but to find a steady, flexible, inheritable home for idle USD. I designed a single-premium USD savings plan: a one-time contribution of US$50****, paid once; income drawdown can begin from year 5 or year 15 depending on future needs (around US$2*** a year if early, around US$4*** if later); cover to age 100, with un-withdrawn amounts continuing to accumulate; whatever isn't used can pass to family as a death benefit. What suits him most is that it's reversible: access it early if needed, or let it keep growing if not. Note: drawdown figures are based on the insurer's illustrative rates, for illustration only, not guaranteed returns — the official policy document prevails.

list.tag: Offence and defence · Growth with a safety net
list.title: A 42-year-old executive open to investing, who also wants a family safety net · Par fund + IUL
list.profile: 42, senior executive, peak earning years, financially literate. Married with children, significant family responsibilities. Has meaningful savings and is open to long-term assets.
list.existing: Complete health cover (hospitalisation, critical illness, accident); some life cover, but still short relative to family responsibilities.
list.risk: Moderate — accepts reasonable investment volatility, provided "the family's safety net comes first."
list.needs: Part of the funds to grow long-term and beat inflation; part to provide high-leverage death cover for the family; growth and protection working in tandem.
list.advice: A two-tool combination with clear roles: (1) a participating (par) fund / savings plan — the steady core, relatively smooth growth, suited to mid-to-long-term funds, around 2*** a year; (2) an Indexed Universal Life (IUL) policy — high-leverage protection plus cash-value growth, turning a manageable outlay into around US$1***** of death cover so that, should the worst happen, the family's life and the children's education aren't disrupted; cash value is index-linked with a floor, participating in upside while protected on the downside, and can be accessed later via policy loans. Why a combination rather than a single product? The par fund handles "steady," the IUL handles "protection plus flexible growth" — matching his offence-and-defence goals exactly. Note: par-fund dividends and cash-value growth are non-guaranteed, depending on the insurer's actual performance — not guaranteed returns; the official policy document prevails.
